summary: If all five fill, the book rotates out of rate-sensitive sleeves (VNQ, IEF, a third of WMT) into Health Care and Staples stocks. Cash ends near 12.2% ($76.41), no position or bucket breaks 15%, and the beta-based 10% stress loss gets slightly worse, from -$22.48 to -$22.71, because EXEL's add (-$1.57) outweighs the sells. The main portfolio-level effect is that Health Care becomes the largest sector bucket at about 14.5%, and two of its three names (INCY and EXEL) are oncology drug makers. Lessons: none in learning.json names the Implicator in applies_to, and the file has no graded Implicator calls. I followed L3's method anyway and made every sector claim by `bucket`, not `screen_label`. Sequencing matters: if the buys fill and the sells don't, cash falls to $24.78 (about 4.0%), well below the 10% buffer the PM has kept.

The realized short-term gain on the third is about $1.5 at the $126.19 stop-block mark, or about $1.8 at the price implied by the packet's market value ($127.47). Small either way.

BND (aggregate index) and TLT (20+ year) track different indexes from IEF, so holding or buying them is not a substantially identical replacement on the usual reading.

That makes Health Care the largest sector bucket, above Staples at 13.9% after P2 and P5 and Consumer Discretionary at 11.2%. Only the US broad ETF bucket (21.4%) is larger.

IDXX (animal diagnostics) is a different business, but it shares the sector tilt and has the highest beta in the bucket (0.831). EXEL is a mid-cap outside the S&P 500, so its look-through overlap with VOO is nil and with VTI is negligible.
